note: 12 bài viết tự soạn (3 đề x 4 mức). Mức A2/B1/B2/C1 do người soạn GÁN theo độ phức tạp cú pháp, vốn từ và mật độ lỗi — chưa có giám khảo con người xác nhận. Dùng để đo độ phân biệt và độ ổn định của bộ chấm, KHÔNG phải thước đo độ chính xác tuyệt đối.

prompts.uniform: Some people think that students should wear school uniforms. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
prompts.remote: Many people now work from home. Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of this trend.
prompts.transport: Some people believe governments should spend more money on public transport than on roads. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

essays.text: I think school uniform is good. Because all student wear same clothes and no one is poor or rich. Also is cheaper for parent. But sometimes uniform is not comfortable in summer is very hot. I like wear my own clothes but I think uniform is better for school. In my school we have uniform and I like it.

In my opinion, school uniforms are a good idea for several reasons. First, they make all students look equal, so nobody feels bad about their clothes. Second, parents don't need to buy many expensive clothes every year. However, some students say uniforms are uncomfortable and they cannot show their personality. I agree that this is a problem, but I think the advantages are more important. So, I think schools should keep uniforms.

While some argue that school uniforms restrict individuality, I largely agree that they should be compulsory. Firstly, uniforms reduce social pressure, as students cannot compete over expensive brands. This creates a more inclusive atmosphere in which pupils can concentrate on their studies. Secondly, uniforms save families money in the long run, because children need fewer outfits. Admittedly, self-expression matters, yet students can still express themselves through hobbies and friendships. In conclusion, the benefits of uniforms outweigh their drawbacks.

The debate over compulsory school uniforms invariably pits the virtue of collective identity against the freedom of self-expression. Although I acknowledge the latter's merit, I am inclined to side with uniforms, chiefly because they neutralise the conspicuous consumption that otherwise taints adolescent peer relations. Where pupils are visibly differentiated by brand, schools inadvertently entrench socioeconomic divides; a standardised dress code, by contrast, levels the field without suppressing character, which tends to find its outlet in conversation, creativity and conduct rather than in clothing. That said, uniforms should be affordable and climate-appropriate, lest the policy itself become a financial burden.

Many people work at home now. It is good because you not need go to office. You can sleep more and no traffic. But is bad too, because you are alone and no talk with friends. Sometimes the children make noise and I can't work. I think work at home is good one or two day in week.

Nowadays more and more people work from home. One advantage is that they save time and money because they don't have to travel to the office. Another advantage is that they can organise their day more freely. On the other hand, working at home can be lonely and some people find it difficult to separate work and private life. In my opinion, the best solution is to work at home some days and in the office on other days.

Remote working has become increasingly common, and it brings both benefits and drawbacks. On the positive side, employees avoid long commutes, which saves time and reduces stress, and employers can cut the cost of office space. Nevertheless, there are notable disadvantages. Workers may feel isolated from colleagues, and the boundary between professional and personal life can blur, leading to burnout. Overall, I believe a hybrid arrangement offers the most sensible balance, since it preserves flexibility without sacrificing teamwork.

The widespread shift towards remote work has been hailed as a liberation from the tyranny of the commute, yet its costs are subtler than its proponents concede. Undoubtedly, flexibility enhances autonomy and, by dispersing the workforce, eases pressure on urban housing and transport. Conversely, the erosion of informal interaction, the corridor conversations from which collaboration and mentoring often spring, can quietly impoverish organisational culture, while the absence of physical boundaries tempts employees to be perpetually available. A deliberately structured hybrid model therefore seems preferable to either extreme.

I think government must spend more money for public transport. Bus and train is good for people because is cheap. Many people have not car. Roads are important too but too many car make air bad and traffic jam. In my city the bus is old and slow, so people don't like it. Government should buy new bus.

I believe governments should spend more money on public transport than on roads. Firstly, public transport is cheaper for ordinary people, and it helps to reduce traffic jams. Secondly, fewer cars means less pollution, which is good for health. Of course, roads are still necessary, for example for ambulances and delivery trucks. But if the government builds more roads, there will be more cars, so the problem will not disappear. For these reasons I agree with the statement.

It is often argued that public funds would be better spent on public transport than on new roads, and I broadly share this view. Building additional roads tends to encourage more car use, so congestion soon returns, whereas efficient buses and trains can move far more people with less pollution. Furthermore, affordable public transport benefits those who cannot afford a car, thereby promoting social equality. However, some investment in roads remains essential, particularly in rural areas where alternatives are scarce. On balance, priority should be given to public transport.

Whether public money is better channelled into public transport or road infrastructure is, in my view, less a question of either/or than of strategic emphasis, though the evidence favours the former. Induced demand ensures that expanded highways are rapidly saturated, rendering them a costly palliative, whereas rail and bus networks deliver durable gains in capacity, emissions and equity of access. Admittedly, rural communities, for whom car ownership is a necessity rather than a choice, cannot be neglected; targeted road maintenance should therefore continue. Nevertheless, the bulk of new expenditure ought to flow to collective transport.
